root_cause: A compromise of a third-party "solver" operator, not the core protocol. Garden's non-custodial design routes swaps through independent solver operators. An attacker got hold of a solver's SSH key, gained root access to its server, and found a private key sitting in an environment variable — then drained that solver's own balances across multiple chains. Garden's core bridge contracts and other users' funds were technically unaffected since solvers are architecturally isolated, but the loss was real and significant.
reason_as_previously_coded: The attacker breached a solver operator's server infrastructure directly, gaining root access through a compromised SSH key, and only then discovered a private key sitting in an environment variable on that compromised machine. Breaching the underlying server infrastructure itself, rather than phishing or socially engineering a specific individual out of their key, is the Infrastructure Hijacking pattern, and for this we have mapped it to Infrastructure Hijacking (IH). Server and cloud infrastructure hosting a bridge operator's secrets falls under the same supporting off-chain infrastructure this domain covers, so for this we have mapped it to FD-5 Governance & Operations.
exclusion_category: Out of scope — no bridge loss
exclusion_rationale: Garden's own incident report states no protocol contracts were compromised and no user funds were at risk; the ~$11.4M were an independent solver's own assets. Mention in text as cross-chain infrastructure risk if useful, but not counted in bridge-loss statistics.

root_cause: After the first CCTP exploit, Pike paused its contracts and shipped an emergency upgrade that added pause() and unpause() functions to the proxy. Those new functions only needed one bit of storage each, but the upgrade assigned them in a way that collided with and overwrote the existing initialized flag, resetting it to its default false value. Four days later, the attacker noticed the contract now looked uninitialized, called its initialize function a second time to set themselves as an active/authorized address, then used that status to call upgradeToAndCall and push their own malicious implementation, draining roughly 479 ETH plus ARB and OP tokens.
reason_as_previously_coded: The emergency patch deployed after the first incident added new pause and unpause functions that shifted the contract's storage layout, silently resetting the initialized flag back to its default, and the attacker exploited that collision to reinitialize the contract and grant themselves admin rights. A storage-layout bug in the contract's own upgrade logic, exploited by using the contract exactly as the flawed code allowed, is the Logic Exploitation pattern, and for this we have mapped it to Logic Exploitation (LE). The flaw let the attacker execute a privileged withdrawal through the contract's own execution path, so for this we have mapped it to FD-4 Execution.
exclusion_rationale: Storage-layout collision in Pike's emergency proxy upgrade (re-initialisation of a lending contract). The exploited component is not a bridge or cross-chain messaging mechanism. (Pike 1st incident, which exploited CCTP message validation, is retained.)

root_cause: Precision Loss: Incorrect rounding in the SwapMath contract's estimateIncrementalLiquidity function caused tick-crossing logic to double-count liquidity at empty tick ranges the attacker deliberately set up, draining low-liquidity pools across 6 chains.
reason_as_previously_coded: The root cause is a precision-loss/rounding bug in the SwapMath contract's estimateIncrementalLiquidity function, which caused the tick-crossing logic to double-count liquidity at empty tick ranges the attacker had deliberately set up. The contract executed its own flawed arithmetic exactly as written, no credential was stolen and no forged proof was submitted. A structural coding flaw exploited by using the contract exactly as designed is the Logic Exploitation pattern, and for this we have mapped it to Logic Exploitation (LE). The flawed calculation lives inside the swap-execution path that directly moves pool liquidity, so for this we have mapped it to FD-4 Execution.
exclusion_rationale: Rounding/precision bug in the KyberSwap Elastic AMM swap math. Multi-chain deployment and separate bridge integrations do not make the AMM exploit a bridge incident.

root_cause: Key Compromise: Suspected Lazarus Group attack drained hot wallet private keys across Ethereum, Tron, and Bitcoin.
reason_as_previously_coded: Suspected Lazarus Group actors obtained the private keys controlling Poloniex's Ethereum, Tron, and Bitcoin hot wallets and used them to authorize withdrawals the exchange's systems had no way of distinguishing from legitimate operator activity. Using a genuinely stolen signing credential to move funds, rather than exploiting a code flaw, is the Credential Seizure pattern, and for this we have mapped it to Credential Seizure (CS). Hot-wallet signing keys sit in the same persistent custodial control plane as bridge validator keys, so for this we have mapped it to FD-5 Governance & Operations.
exclusion_rationale: Centralized-exchange hot-wallet private-key compromise. No bridge or cross-chain messaging mechanism involved.

root_cause: Cloud Provider Hack: Attackers breached the database of Mixin Network's cloud service provider, exposing custody-layer material and enabling unauthorized withdrawal of network assets.
reason_as_previously_coded: The attacker breached the database of Mixin Network's cloud infrastructure provider directly, rather than phishing a specific individual or exploiting an on-chain contract, exposing the custody-layer material needed to move network assets. Compromising the underlying cloud/database infrastructure itself is the Infrastructure Hijacking pattern, and for this we have mapped it to Infrastructure Hijacking (IH). Cloud infrastructure hosting a network's custody and signing material falls under the same supporting off-chain infrastructure this domain covers, so for this we have mapped it to FD-5 Governance & Operations.
exclusion_category: Out of scope — custodial network infrastructure
exclusion_rationale: Compromise of Mixin's cloud service provider database (custodial hot-wallet material). The exploited component cannot be tied to a bridge transfer/verification mechanism; under a bridge-only inclusion rule it is excluded.

root_cause: Key Exploit: Unauthorized transactions drained ETH/BSC/Polygon hot wallets; the FBI attributed the theft to North Korea's Lazarus Group. Stake's co-founder said a transaction-authorization service, not raw private keys, was the compromised component.
reason_as_previously_coded: Attackers gained unauthorized access to the signing/authorization layer behind Stake.com's ETH, BSC, and Polygon hot wallets and used it to move funds out with no interaction with any smart contract; the FBI attributed the theft to the Lazarus Group. Using compromised signing access to authorize a transaction, rather than exploiting a code flaw, is the Credential Seizure pattern, and for this we have mapped it to Credential Seizure (CS). Hot-wallet signing credentials are part of the persistent operational control plane, so for this we have mapped it to FD-5 Governance & Operations.
exclusion_rationale: Theft from an online casino/betting platform's hot wallets (FBI: Lazarus). Funds moving across several chains does not make it a bridge attack.

root_cause: Integer Overflow: The CreateMassPools function's getArraySum summation overflowed uint256 in the unaudited LockedControl.sol vesting contract, letting the attacker record a deposit far larger than what was actually transferred, then withdraw the inflated balance.
reason_as_previously_coded: The root cause is an arithmetic overflow in the unaudited LockedControl.sol vesting contract's getArraySum function: passing values that summed past uint256's ceiling wrapped the total to a tiny number, letting the attacker record a deposit far larger than what was actually transferred. The contract executed this flawed arithmetic exactly as written, no credential was stolen and no forged proof was submitted. A structural coding flaw exploited by using the contract exactly as designed is the Logic Exploitation pattern, and for this we have mapped it to Logic Exploitation (LE). The flawed calculation lives inside the function that actually executes the token withdrawal, so for this we have mapped it to FD-4 Execution.
exclusion_rationale: Integer overflow in Poolz Finance's LockedControl token-vesting/locker contract. The exploited component is not a bridge or cross-chain messaging mechanism.
